parole.testo: Borrowed from French -isme.
Borrowed from French absinthe.
Borrowed from French avers, from Latin adversus.
Borrowed from French autoritarisme, from Latin auctōritās. With -и́зм (-ízm) suffix.
Borrowed from French agrégat, further from Latin aggregātus.
Borrowed from French agression. Further from Latin aggressiō.

Borrowed from French acteur, further from Latin āctor. Compare natively formed Macedonian глумец (glumec), Serbo-Croatian глумац (akin to глум (glum), глуми́ться (glumítʹsja)); Slovene igralec, Czech herec (akin to игра́ (igrá), игра́ть (igrátʹ)).
Borrowed from French accise, from Latin accisus. Attested since the time of Peter the Great.
Borrowed from French alliance. Further from Latin alligō (ad- + ligō). Compare typologically Russian сою́з (sojúz) (akin to вяза́ть (vjazátʹ), у́зы (úzy)).

parole.significato: type, theatrical character, line, (figuratively) part, role
parole.testo: Borrowed from French emploi. Further from Latin implicō. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ-.
Borrowed from French annihilation, from Latin annihilātio.
Borrowed from French annonce. Ultimately from Latin nūntius. Doublet of денонса́ция (denonsácija), ну́нций (núncij), and проно́нс (pronóns).

parole.significato: full-face, face on (with the face to the viewer, pointing straight ahead)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French en face. Omitting several steps, from Latin in + Latin faciēs.

Borrowed from French apéritif (whence multiple borrowings: Bulgarian аперитив (aperitiv), Czech aperitiv, Polish aperitif, Serbo-Croatian аперитив, and many more), from Latin aperitīvus (variant of apertīvus) < aperiō.
Borrowed from French Arabe, from Latin Arabus.
Borrowed from French arbitre, from Latin arbiter.
Borrowed from French arbitrage. Further from Latin arbitror + -āticum.
Borrowed from French article, from Latin articulus. Doublet of арти́кул (artíkul).
Borrowed from French artiste. First attested in 1775 . Ultimately from Latin ars.

parole.significato: postgraduate, graduate student (a person continuing to study after completing a degree)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aspirant.
Borrowed from French asphalte, from Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”).

Borrowed from French atelier. Further from Latin assula (a diminutive of axis / assis (“axis, wheel, axle”)). Can be calqued as **стру́жечная. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (whence also ось (osʹ)). Compare typologically Latin arēna (harēna) (whence аре́на (aréna)).
Borrowed from French affiche. Further from Latin ad- + Latin fīgō (via Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre).
Borrowed from French base.

Borrowed from French banal + -ный (-nyj). Further from Latin bannālis, from Latin bannus (whence also English abandon). Further from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (whence also English ban). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”).
Borrowed from French barge. Ultimately from Latin barca. Doublet of ба́рка (bárka) and барка́с (barkás).
Borrowed from French bécasse. Further from Latin beccus (whence also English beak) + -āceus.
Borrowed from French bémol (“b soft”). Ultimately from Latin mollis.
First attested in 1866. бес- (bes-) + фо́рма (fórma) + -енный (-ennyj), a calque of French amorphe or Latin amorphus.
Borrowed from French billet. Ultimately from Latin bulla.
Borrowed from French boa, from Latin boa.

Borrowed from French boucle (“loop; buckle; curl of hair”) in the mid-18th century, from Old French boucle (“buckle”), from Latin buccula (“cheek strap of a helmet”), diminutive of bucca (“puffed cheek; mouth”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: broth, bouillon (water in which food (meat or vegetable etc) has been boiled)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bouillon. Ultimately from Latin bulliō from Latin bulla.

parole.significato: bust (sculptural portrayal of a person's head and shoulders)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French buste. Further from Latin bustum (via Italian). Further akin to Latin ūrō. For the meaning development compare ту́мба (túmba) (< Latin tumba, whence also English tomb). Compare natively formed Czech poprsí, Polish popiersie «**по́персь», «**попе́рсье».
Borrowed from French vase, from Latin vas.
Borrowed from French variante. Further from Latin variāns, p.p.p. of variō (< varius). Compare natively formed Czech provedení, Slovene različica.
Borrowed from French vassal, further from Latin vassallus.
Borrowed from French vitrage. Further from Latin vitrum (whence also витри́на (vitrína)).
Borrowed from French vitrine. Further from Latin vitrum (whence also витра́ж (vitráž)). Compare natively formed Czech výkladec, Macedonian излог (izlog).
Borrowed from French volière. Omitting several steps, from Latin volō + -ārius.
Borrowed from French voyage, further from Latin viāticum, from Latin viāticus, from Latin via + -āticus.
Borrowed from French héros, from Latin hērōs, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs, “demi-god, hero”). Influenced by the displaced earlier иро́й (irój), directly from the Greek. Cognate with English hero.
Borrowed from French glande, from Latin glans (“acorn”).
Borrowed from French dame (possibly via Polish dama), from Latin domina (“lady”), from domus (“house”), from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm, from root Proto-Indo-European *dem- (“to build”).
Borrowed from French débile, from Latin dēbilis.
Borrowed from French devise. Ultimately from Latin dīvidō. Doublet of дефи́с (defís), дивиде́нд (dividénd), and диви́зия (divízija).
Borrowed from French décorum, from Latin decōrus (“proper, decent”).

Borrowed from French détail, from détailler (“to set apart”). Further from Latin de- + Latin tāliō. Attested since the middle of 19th century. Compare typologically подро́бность (podróbnostʹ) (akin to дроби́ть (drobítʹ)).
Borrowed from French déterminatif, from Latin dētermināre.

Pseudo-Gallicism; from диве́рсия (divérsija, “subversion”) + -ант (-ant, agent suffix), with the first element borrowed ultimately from Latin dīversiōnem, via one or several western intermediaries (cf. Polish dywersja, French diversion), and with the second element borrowed from French -ant. No such

Borrowed from French dirigeable. Some steps omitting, from Latin dīrigō (whence also Russian дирижёр (dirižór), дирижи́ровать (dirižírovatʹ); also дире́ктор (diréktor), директи́ва (direktíva) (< p.p.p. dīrēctus)) + Latin -abilis, i.e. directable.
Borrowed from French dossier. Ultimately from Latin dorsum, whence also English endorse.

Borrowed from French douzaine (“twelve”), from Latin duodecim (“twelve”), from duo (“two”) + decem (“ten”) (via PIE componentwise cognate with двена́дцать (dvenádcatʹ)). Influenced by дю́жий (djúžij).

parole.significato: gesture (communicative motion of the limbs or body)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French geste, from Latin gestus.

parole.significato: token; coin (e.g. in a casino), chip
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jeton. Further from Latin iectō (< Latin iaciō, akin to iaceō), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)yeh₁-.
Borrowed from French jongleur. Further from Latin ioculor.

Borrowed from French journal (which also calqued into дневни́к (dnevník)). Further from Latin diurnālis, from diurnus, close akin to diurnum (whence French jour, whence дежу́рный (dežúrnyj)). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyew- (whence день (denʹ), ди́во (dívo)).
Borrowed from French initiative, ultimately from Latin initiō, from Latin initium, from Latin ineō (in- + eō).
From French intérieur, itself from Latin interior.
Calque of French exclusif, ultimately a calque of Latin exclūsīvus. By surface analysis, исключи́ть (isključítʹ) + -тельный (-telʹnyj). Doublet of эксклюзи́вный (ekskljuzívnyj).
Borrowed probably from French hystérique, from Latin hysterica passiō, from Ancient Greek ὑστέρα (hustéra), feminine of ὕστερος (hústeros), from Proto-Indo-European *udero-.

Borrowed from French histoire, remodelled with an awareness of Latin historia or Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía), from Ancient Greek ἵστωρ (hístōr), from Proto-Indo-European *wéydtōr, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-.

parole.significato: long underwear, long johns, that is worn either under normal clothing in cold weather, or as a night dress.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French caleçon. Further from Latin calceus from Latin calx.
Borrowed from French candélabre, from Latin candēlābrum.
Borrowed from French capote. Further from Latin cappa. Doublet of капюшо́н (kapjušón), капу́т (kapút), ке́пка (képka), and ша́пка (šápka).

parole.significato: percussion cap, fulminate cap, detonator, primer (metal cap on muzzleloading firearms)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French capsule, from Latin capsula. Doublet of ка́псула (kápsula).
Borrowed from French capuchon. Omitting several steps, from Latin cappa. Doublet of капо́т (kapót), капу́т (kapút), капуци́н (kapucín), капучи́но (kapučíno), ке́пка (képka), and ша́пка (šápka).
Borrowed from French carrière. Further from Latin carrāria, from Latin carrus.
Borrowed from French clerc, itself derived from Latin clericus. Attested since the 18th century.
Borrowed from French combinaison (“overalls”). Further from Latin combīnātiō, whence also комбина́ция (kombinácija).
Borrowed from French commerçant. Omitting several steps, from Latin commercium (whence комме́рция (kommércija)).
Borrowed from French contrôle. Further from Latin contra- + Latin rotula, from Latin rota.

Via French cosmopolite from Latin cosmopolītēs from Koine Greek κοσμοπολίτης (kosmopolítēs, “citizen of the world”), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”). (slur): Used since the Soviet 1948 anti-cosmopolitan campaign, from the propaganda trope безродный космопол

Borrowed from French cosmopolitisme from Latin cosmopolītēs, cosmopolītismus from Koine Greek κοσμοπολίτης (kosmopolítēs, “citizen of the world”), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”).

parole.significato: suit (suit of clothes, men’s suit or women’s suit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French costume, ultimately from Latin cōnsuētūdō.
Borrowed from French côtelette. Further from Latin costa + -ellus + -ittus.

Connected to French cauchemar, from Middle French cauchemare, from Old French cauquemare. First element from Latin calcare (“to trample, tread on”); second element from Middle Dutch mare (“phantom, spirit, nightmare”), from Proto-Germanic *marǭ (“nightmare, incubus”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-

parole.significato: cretin, idiot (inconsiderate or mean spirited person)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French crétin. Further from Latin Chrīstiānus. Doublet of крестья́нин (krestʹjánin).
Via French critique from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós).

parole.significato: croissant (a flaky roll or pastry in a form of a crescent)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French croissant.
Borrowed from French croûton. Further from Latin crusta.

Borrowed from French courante. Sense development: “music” → “chimes” → “chiming clock”. Omitting several steps, from Latin currō (i.e. **бегунки). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers-. Compare typologically хо́дики (xódiki) (akin ходи́ть (xodítʹ)).

Borrowed from French courier. Omitting several steps, from Latin currō (i.e. бегуно́к (begunók)). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers-. Compare typologically на побегу́шках (na pobegúškax), побегу́шечник (pobegúšečnik), побегу́шник (pobegúšnik). Also compare гоне́ц (gonéc).
Borrowed from French couturier. Omitting several steps, from Latin consuō + -tūra + -ārius.
Borrowed from French cuvette. Further from Latin cūpa + -ittus.
From French langouste, from Latin locusta.

parole.significato: livery (in bourgeois houses and courts, the uniforms of a special cut and a certain color for waiters, porters, coachme…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French livrée. Ultimately from Latin līber. Doublet of либера́льный (liberálʹnyj). Akin to Russian лю́ди (ljúdi).
Borrowed from French liqueur, from Latin liquor.
Borrowed from French lieue. Further from Latin leuga. Doublet of (unit of distantce) ли́га (líga) .
Borrowed from French manège. Omitting several steps, from Latin manus.
Borrowed from French mat, probably from Latin mattus.
Borrowed from French mémoires, plural of mémoire. Ultimately from Latin memoria (whence also English memory), further from Latin memor.
Borrowed from French mètre.
Borrowed from French mollusque. Omitting several steps, from Latin mollis.
Borrowed from French moraliste. Further from Latin mōrālis.
From French motivation, ultimately from Latin mōtīvus.
Borrowed from French maire. Further from Latin maior. Doublet of майо́р (majór).

Borrowed from French maître. Further from Latin magister. Doublet of маги́стр (magístr), ма́стер (máster), маэ́стро (maéstro), and ми́стер (míster). From the Latin term the second component of гроссме́йстер (grossméjster) is also derived.
Borrowed from French néophyte, from Latin neophytus, from Koine Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos, “newly planted, (figuratively) new convert”). Piecewise root cognate with новоприбы́вший (novopribývšij).
Borrowed from French niche. Further from Latin nīdus. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós (whence also Russian гнездо́ (gnezdó), English nest).
Borrowed from French nocturne. Ultimately from Latin nocturnus, further from Latin nox, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
Borrowed from French nuance (“nuance, shade, hue”). Omitting several steps, from Latin nūbēs. Compare typologically Italian sfumatura (<< Latin fūmus).
Borrowed from French oculaire, from Latin oculāris (compare English ocular).
Borrowed from French officiant. Further from Latin officiō.
Borrowed from French pas. Further from Latin passus (whence also пасса́ж (passáž), English pace, among others).
Borrowed from French pension. Omitting several steps, from Latin pendō.

Borrowed from French parasite. Further from Latin parasītus, from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos), from παρά (pará) + σῖτος (sîtos). Compare typologically нахле́бник (naxlébnik) (< хлеб (xleb)). Compare natively formed Czech cizopasník, i.e. **чужепасник (akin to чужо́й (čužój) and пасти́ (pastí

parole.significato: arcade, passage (covered passage, usually with shops on both sides)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French passage. Further from Latin passus (<~ pandō + -tus) + -āre + -āticum.
Borrowed from French patron. Further from Latin patrōnus (the same as above).
Borrowed from French patronage. Further from Latin patrōnus + -āticum.
Borrowed from French pensionnaire. Omitting several steps, from Latin pēnsiō (whence пе́нсия (pénsija)) + Latin -arius. Further from Latin pendō.

parole.significato: peignoir (a long outer garment for women)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French peignoir. Further from Latin pectinō, from Latin pecten (akin to pectō). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ-. Compare typologically дерю́га (derjúga) (akin to драть (dratʹ)). For another descendant of PIE *peḱ- (“to pluck (wool, hair)”), фехтова́ть (fextovátʹ), note дра́ть
Borrowed from French plan from Latin planus, possibly via Polish plan or German Plan.
Borrowed from French pluralisme. Analyzable as Latin plūrālis + -и́зм (-ízm).
Borrowed from French plage. Further from Latin plagia, from Ancient Greek πλάγιος (plágios), from πλάγος (plágos) + -ιος (-ios).
From French chauffer. Omitting several steps, from Latin calefaciō. Compare typologically горячи́тельный напи́ток (gorjačítelʹnyj napítok).
Borrowed from French polype, from Latin polypus, from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous).

Borrowed from French porte-monnaie. Ultimately from Latin portō (whence multiple descendants, compare close related English portfolio, Russian портфе́ль (portfélʹ), Russian портфо́лио (portfólio)) + Latin monēta (whence English money, English mint, Russian моне́та (monéta)).

Borrowed from French porte-épée (“swordbelt”). Ultimately from Latin portō (whence multiple descendants, compare close related English portfolio, Russian портфе́ль (portfélʹ), Russian портфо́лио (portfólio)) + Latin spatha (whence English spade, Russian шпа́га (špága)), further from Ancient Greek σπ
Borrowed from French poète, from Latin poēta, itself from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs). Doublet of пии́т (piít) and пии́та (piíta).

parole.significato: president (the head of state of a republic, the primary leader of a corporation, male or female)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French président, from Latin praesidens.
Borrowed from French press. Further from Latin pressō (frequentative of premō).
From French prostitution, itself from Latin prostitutio. Attested since the 19th century.
Borrowed from French procédure, from Latin procedere (“to go forward, proceed”).
Borrowed from French pair. Further from Latin pār.
Borrowed from French pupitre. Further from Latin pulpitum.
Borrowed from French purée. Ultimately from Latin pūrus (whence ultimately also English pure, Russian пури́зм (purízm)), further from Proto-Indo-European *pewH- (whence also Latin putus, Latin pius).
Borrowed from French ragoût. Further from Latin regustō, from Latin re- + gustō, akin to Latin gustus. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews-.
From French raccourci (“shortcut; foreshortening”). Omitting several steps, from Latin re- + ad- + Latin curtus.
Borrowed from French raison, from Latin ratiōnem. Doublet of рацио́н (ración).
Borrowed from French répertoire. Further from Latin repertōrium.
Borrowed from French restaurant. Further from Latin restaurō (via p.a.p. restaurāns).

parole.significato: resource (something that one uses to achieve an objective)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ressource, further from Latin resurgō.
Borrowed from French rétrospective. Omitting several steps, from Latin retrōspectus, p.p.p. of retrōspiciō.
From реши́ть (rešítʹ) + -тельный (-telʹnyj), a calque of French résolu, ultimately from Latin resolūtus.
Borrowed from French rôle, from Latin rotulus (“paper scroll (for actors)”).
Borrowed from French royal. Further from Latin rēgālis.
Borrowed from French sachet, further from Latin saccus + -ittus.
Borrowed from French saison, from Latin satiōnem.
Borrowed from French semestre, from Latin sēmēstris.
Borrowed from French cider, from Latin sicera, from Ancient Greek σίκερα (síkera), of Semitic origin.
Borrowed from French sommelier, ultimately from Latin sagma.
Borrowed from French sorte, from Latin sors, sortis.
PIE word  *sḗh₂l From French saucisse + -ка (-ka). Ultimately from Latin sāl.

PIE word  *sḗh₂l Borrowed from French sauce. Further from Latin salsus (akin to sāl). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sḗh₂l (whence also Russian соль (solʹ), Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls), English salt).
Borrowed from French spectacle, from Latin spectaculum.
Borrowed from French spectre, from Latin spectrum.
Borrowed from French stratosphère; further from Latin strātum (“bed, couch”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”).
Borrowed from French souvenir, from Latin subvenīre.
Borrowed from French soupe. Further from Latin suppa.

Borrowed from French souteneur (“pimp, supporter”) (whence also Bulgarian сутеньор (sutenjor), literally “поддерживатель”, also compare German Zuhälter), from soutenir (whence also Bulgarian сутиен (sutien)). Omitting several steps, from Latin sustineō (whence also English sustain).
Borrowed from French sujet, from Latin subiectum/subjectum. Doublet of субъе́кт (subʺjékt).

Borrowed from French suite. Omitting several steps, from Latin sequor, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Doublet of сви́та (svíta). Via Latin also cognate with секу́нда (sekúnda).
Borrowed from French taverne. Ultimately from Latin trabs.

Borrowed from French théâtre, from Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron) (a verbal noun of θεάομαι (theáomai)). Displaced феа́тр (feátr), which had been borrowed from the Byzantine Greek. Compare natively formed Czech divadlo (i.e **дива́ло, akin to диви́ться (divítʹsja)); Serbo-Croa

parole.significato: volume (of a book, magazine or disk)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tome, from Latin tomus, from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos), from Ancient Greek τέμνω (témnō). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *temh₁- (whence also Proto-Slavic *tęti, Latin temnō, tondeō, and possibly tempus, templum).
Borrowed from French tour, from Latin turris (“tower; rook”) (whence also English tower, English turret). Doublet of туре́ль (turélʹ). Compare also Ukrainian тура (tura).
Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbo, turbinem (“circular movement, top, reel, spindle”).
Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbō (“circular movement”) + наддува́ть (nadduvátʹ, “to pressurize by blowing”), from над- (nad-, “over”) + дуть (dutʹ, “to blow”).
Borrowed from French tulle, from French Tulle, a town named after Latin Tūtēla (a Roman deity), from Latin tūtēla, from Latin tueor.
Borrowed from French unitaire, from unité + -aire, from Latin ūnitās.
Borrowed from French phare. Further from Latin pharus, from Ancient Greek Φάρος (Pháros). Compare natively formed Czech světlomet, i.e. **светломёт, Slovene žaromet, i.e. **жаромёт.
Borrowed from French farce (“stuffing”) and farcir (“to stuff”). Further from Latin farciō. First attested 18th century. Doublet of фарс (fars).
Borrowed from French face (“face, front part”). Further from Latin faciēs (whence English face).
Borrowed from French façade. Omitting several steps, from Latin faciēs (whence also English face).
Borrowed from French façon < Old French façon (whence also English fashion). Further from Latin factiōnem < Latin faciō.
Borrowed from French fat, Latin fatuus (“stupid”).
Borrowed from French fédération.
Borrowed from French fellation, from Latin fellatio.

parole.significato: lobby, foyer (in a theater, cinema, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French foyer. Omitting several steps, from Latin focus.
Borrowed from French fondue. Omitting several steps, from Latin fundō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd-, extended from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰew-.
Borrowed from French forme, from Latin fōrma.

parole.significato: fort (fortified defensive structure stationed with troops)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fort. Further from Latin fortis.
Borrowed from French fougasse. Omitting several steps, from Latin focus.
Borrowed from French funiculaire. Further from Latin fūniculus + -ārius.

parole.significato: portable loading room, van, caravan, wagon, waggon, camion (a covered vehicle used for carrying goods)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fourgon. Further from Latin fūror, from Latin fūr. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (whence Russian брать (bratʹ)). Noncognate with Russian фу́ра (fúra) (which is паро́м (paróm) related instead).
Borrowed from French fuselage. Ultimately from Latin fūsus. Compare Russian веретенообра́зный (veretenoobráznyj).

parole.significato: chance, prospect (chance for advancement, progress or profit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chance, from Latin *cadentia (cadēns (p.a.p. of cadō) + -ia).
Borrowed from French chansonnier, ultimately from Latin canō.

parole.significato: blackmail (payment of money exacted by means of intimidation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chantage, ultimately from Latin canō.
Borrowed from French châssis. Ultimately from Latin capsa. Doublet of ка́псула (kápsula), ка́псюль (kápsjulʹ), ка́сса (kássa), and кассе́та (kasséta).
Borrowed from French château, from Middle French chasteau, chastel, from Old French chastel, from Latin castellum.
Borrowed from French chevelure. Omitting several steps, from Latin capillus (whence also Russian капилля́р (kapilljár)).
Borrowed from French chef. Omitting several steps, from Latin caput (whence also капита́н (kapitán)).

parole.significato: driver (of an automobile, truck, bus, etc.; usually a paid professional)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chauffeur (literally “stoker, fireman”). Omitting several steps, from Latin calefaciō + -ātor/-tor.
From French évacuation, from Latin evacuatio.
Borrowed from French existentialisme, from Latin existentia.
